q: This is the synoptic picture at noon. Where does the wind come from at your position?
a: From about WSW
o: From about ENE
From about S
From about N
why: In the north air circles a low anticlockwise, angled in towards the centre: south of it the wind is about WSW.
ref: Pressure systems — wind round a low

q: You want to know where the low centre lies. Where is it?
a: On your left, a little ahead — NNW
o: On your right, a little ahead — E
Straight ahead of you — NE
On your left, a little behind — W
why: Buys Ballot: back to the wind, the low is on your left in the north — a little ahead, as the wind angles in.

fig.title: No forecast for two days
lines: You stand with your back to the wind

q: Nothing else changes between the two charts. What mean wind do you plan for at 1200?
a: About 24 kn — F6
o: About 6 kn — F2
About 12 kn — F4
About 48 kn — F10
why: Wind goes inversely with isobar spacing: half the spacing, twice the wind — 12 × 120/60 = 24 kn, force 6.

fig.title: Two synoptic charts
lines: Isobars every 4 hPa in your area

q: You are where the boat is drawn, on the east side of this high. Where does the wind come from?
a: From about NNW
o: From about SSE
From about W
From about E
why: Round a high in the north air turns clockwise and slightly outwards: on its east side the wind is about NNW.
ref: Pressure systems — wind round a high

q: You are planning the week from this chart. Where is this low in its life?
a: Occluded and mature — it will slowly fill
o: A young wave — it will deepen fast now
Just forming — a new low on the front
Still deepening — the warm sector widens
why: When the cold front catches the warm front the low occludes: its deepening is over and it begins to fill.

fig.title: Synoptic chart, 1200 UTC
lines: Cold front has caught the warm front

q: You are on a day sail along the coast. What is coming, and what follows it?
a: A warm front — rain, poorer visibility, then a veer
o: A cold front — squalls, then clear cold air
A ridge — the cloud will clear by evening
A sea breeze — the wind dies at sunset
why: Cirrus, a halo, lowering altostratus, a falling glass and a backing wind: the classic approach of a warm front.

q: You kept the log through the afternoon. What happened between 1600 and 1900?
a: The warm front passed — you are in the warm sector
o: The cold front passed — the low is behind you
The low centre passed overhead — it will clear
An occlusion passed — the wind will now die
why: As a warm front passes the rain eases to drizzle, the wind veers, the glass stops falling and the air turns warm and damp.

q: You will be at sea when the front arrives. What does the front itself bring?
a: Squalls and heavy rain, a sharp veer, the glass rising
o: Hours of steady rain and a slow back to SE
A slow clearance and the wind dying to calm
Thickening fog and a back to the south
why: A cold front brings a line of squalls and heavy rain, a sudden veer to W or NW and a rising barometer.

q: You need a quiet night at anchor off this island. Where do you go?
a: A — the east side, in the lee of W and NW
o: C — the north side, best shelter from the S
B — the west side, clear of the southerly sea
Off the south beach, then move at midnight
why: Veering is clockwise: S to W to NW puts B and C on a lee shore tonight, while the east side is sheltered from it.

fig.note: Forecast: S 5, veering W then NW 6 tonight

q: The centre passes south of you during the night. How does the wind shift?
a: It backs through E and NE to N
o: It veers through S and SW to W
It stays SE and dies as it passes
It veers to S, then backs to E
why: With the low passing to the south of you the wind backs: anticlockwise, from SE through E and NE to N.

q: There is no front on the chart. What do you prepare for at about 1500?
a: Squalls and a sudden veer as the trough passes
o: A slow back to S with steady rain
Nothing much — without a front it stays mild
A slow fall to calm as the pressure rises
why: A trough is a line of low pressure: like a weak front it brings showers, squalls and a sharp veer as it passes.

q: When do you sail the leg?
a: At first light, to be in by mid-afternoon
o: Tonight, on the easing NW wind
Mid-afternoon, once the ridge settles
Tomorrow evening, on the new S breeze
why: A ridge between two lows gives a short fair spell: use it early, because the next low's wind follows quickly.

q: Your crew says the main low is too far away to matter. What do you tell them?
a: The secondary may bring the strongest wind of all
o: A secondary is always weaker than the main low
At 1002 hPa the secondary is too high to matter
A secondary fills before it reaches the Channel
why: A secondary low on the trailing front can deepen fast and bring gales stronger than the primary's.

q: You are 15 M out on a coastal passage. What does the log tell you?
a: A fast fall — strong wind or a gale is near
o: A normal swing — nothing to note yet
A slow fall — a little rain later today
A fall that means the low has passed
why: 6 hPa in 3 hours is well past the 3 hPa warning sign: expect strong wind or a gale within hours.

q: Your crew wants to leave at 0600 now that the glass is rising. What do you say?
a: Wait — a fast rise brings strong wind for hours
o: Go — a rising glass always means less wind
Go — the low has passed, the sea drops at once
Wait — the glass will fall again within the hour
why: A quick rise behind a low means a steep gradient: strong, gusty NW wind for some hours yet.

fig.title: Night at anchor, a low passing

q: You write the wind in the log. What force is it?
a: Force 7 — near gale
o: Force 6 — strong breeze
Force 8 — gale
Force 9 — severe gale
why: Beaufort goes by the mean wind: 28–33 kn is force 7. Log the gusts beside it.

fig.title: Wind instrument, 10-minute mean
lines: Sea heaps up, foam blown in streaks

q: What wave height do you plan for on the open leg?
a: 2.5 to 4 m
o: 4 to 6 m
why: Forecast terms: slight 0.5–1.25 m, moderate 1.25–2.5 m, rough 2.5–4 m, very rough 4–6 m.

q: How will the sea change during your crossing?
a: It keeps building — the wind is still young
o: It peaks at once — the fetch alone sets it
It eases as the wind settles in
It stays slight — 80 M is a short fetch
why: Waves grow with wind strength, fetch and duration: a new force 6 over 80 M of open water builds the sea for hours.

fig.title: Crossing the gulf
lines: N 6 set in at 0600 after a calm
Open water to the N: 80 M

q: You plan a leg down the open coast tomorrow. What does the swell tell you?
a: A deep low far to the NW — get a fresh forecast
o: Nothing — swell only follows the local wind
A sea breeze is building from the NW
The high is strengthening over you
why: Long-period swell runs far ahead of a deep low: get the latest forecast before any open-coast leg.

fig.title: Galicia, September, 0800
lines: New long swell from the NW, 14 s

q: When and how do you round the Bill?
a: Near slack water, well outside the race
o: At the peak of the fair SW-going stream
In the foul stream, close under the cliffs
Any time — a race only runs at neaps
why: The fair stream runs against the wind: SW 6 over 4 kn makes the race dangerous. Round near slack and give it a wide berth.

fig.title: Bound SW round the Bill
lines: Race off the Bill: 4 kn at springs

q: How will the breeze behave through the afternoon?
a: Build to F3–4, veer a little, die at dusk
o: Back a little and build through the night
Die by 1300 as the land heats up
Swing off the land by 1500 and freshen
why: A sea breeze builds as the land heats, peaks in mid-afternoon, veers through the day in the north and dies at sunset.

fig.title: Turkish coast, July, settled
lines: Coast runs E–W, open sea to the S

q: You are anchored at A in midsummer, in settled weather. How will this breeze change after sunrise?
a: It dies, then a sea breeze sets in from the S
o: It builds to F5 from the N by noon
It veers to the E and builds all day
It holds all day — it is the gradient wind
why: A land breeze blows off the cool land at night and dies as the sun heats it; by late morning the sea breeze takes over.

q: What is this wind, and when will it ease?
a: Katabatic — it eases after sunrise
o: Anabatic — it builds until sunrise
A sea breeze — it eases at noon
Gradient wind — it lasts until a front
why: On clear nights cold air slides down the slopes: a katabatic wind, strongest before dawn, gone once the sun warms them.

fig.title: Gulf of Kotor, April, 0200
lines: Clear, starry sky, no gradient wind
Steep slopes, snow on the peaks
Gusts to F5 pouring off the mountains

q: Why is it blowing harder than forecast close inshore?
a: Anabatic flow up the hot slopes adds to it
o: Katabatic flow down the slopes adds to it
A land breeze off the slopes adds to it
Funnelling between two islands adds to it
why: On sunny afternoons warm air rises up the slopes — an anabatic wind — and strengthens the onshore sea breeze.

fig.title: Sunny afternoon, south coast of Crete
lines: Steep sun-baked slopes above the shore
Close inshore: S 4–5, towards the hills

q: You plan to motor-sail through the strait at A. What wind do you expect there?
a: Stronger, blowing along the strait from N
o: Weaker, sheltered by the islands each side
The same NE 5 as in the open sea
Stronger, blowing across the strait from E
why: A strait between high land squeezes and turns the wind: it blows along the channel, and harder than outside.

q: You are bound east along this coast. Where do you expect the most wind and the worst sea?
a: A — off the tip of the headland
o: B — in open water, clear of the land
C — in the bay past the headland
Equal at A, B and C — same gradient
why: Wind bends and speeds up round a headland, and the stream runs hardest there: expect more wind and a confused sea off the tip.

q: You motor west in calm water at A, close under the cliffs, heading for B. How do you set up?
a: Reef before B — the full N 6 returns there
o: Set full sail at A to use the first puffs
Full sail — the lee reaches well past B
Keep close under the cliffs — no gusts there
why: A high island casts a wind shadow, but its edge is sharp: the full wind returns at once, and gusts fall off the cliffs.

q: You plan the coming days in the Cyclades. What do you expect?
a: Meltemi — N 6–7 under clear skies
o: Sirocco — S 5–6 with haze and rain
Light sea breezes only, as under a high
A S gale ahead of a cold front
why: High over the Balkans, low over Turkey: the gradient drives the Meltemi, N in the Cyclades, often force 6–7 for days.

fig.title: Synoptic chart, late July
lines: Isobars run N–S over the Aegean

q: Kvarner, January. Where do you spend the night?
a: B — in the lee of the island, to its SW
o: A — under the mainland, which is upwind
A — the channel is too narrow for a sea
Either — the Bora always dies at night
why: The Bora falls off the mountains in violent gusts, worst right under them: shelter behind an island, well away from them.

fig.note: Forecast: Bora NE 7, gusts 50 kn, tonight

q: Which wind is setting in, and how will it develop?
a: Sirocco — builds over a day or two, big SE seas
o: Bora — sudden NE gusts within the hour
Mistral — cold NW wind under clear skies
Meltemi — N 6 by afternoon, then calm
why: Hazy humid air, Saharan dust and a slowly building SE wind: the Sirocco (Jugo), raising long seas up the Adriatic.

fig.title: Southern Adriatic, October
lines: Red dust on deck after a shower

q: Your crew says the sky is perfect and the wind is fair. What do you decide?
a: Stay — a Mistral is building to NW 7–8
o: Go — the front has passed, it will settle
Go — a NW wind is fair for going east
Go after the sea breeze sets in at noon
why: High over Biscay and low over Genoa after a cold front: the Mistral, NW 7–8 or more under clear skies, often for days.

fig.title: Port-Camargue, April, 0700
lines: Sky clear, air cold and dry, NW 4
Plan: 40 M E across the open gulf

q: Which wind is this, and what does the strait do to it?
a: Levante — the strait squeezes and speeds it
o: Poniente — the strait turns it to the E
Sirocco — it blows across from Africa
Mistral — it pours down from the Pyrenees
why: The Levante is the E wind of the Alborán Sea; the strait funnels it, so it blows far harder there than outside.

fig.title: Estepona, bound W for Cádiz
lines: Cloud banner streaming W off the Rock
Málaga: E 3; in the strait: E 6–7

q: You are choosing a berth for the night. From which direction must it be sheltered?
a: North-east
o: South-west
South-east
North-west
why: Poyraz is the Turkish name for the NE wind — cold and strong in winter in the Marmara and the north Aegean.

q: Your crew hopes the breeze will blow the fog away. Will it?
a: No — sea fog lasts until the air mass changes
o: Yes — any wind over F3 clears fog
Yes — the sun will burn it off by noon
No — but it will lift at dusk as it cools
why: Warm moist air over a colder sea makes advection (sea) fog: wind does not clear it — only a change of air mass does.

q: You want to leave for a 20-mile coastal leg. When will the fog clear?
a: By mid-morning, as the sun warms the land
o: Not until a front brings new air
Only at nightfall, as the air cools
Not today — it drifts out and thickens
why: Radiation fog forms over land on clear calm nights and burns off as the sun warms the ground, usually by mid-morning.

fig.title: River harbour, October, 0700
lines: Thick fog over the river and town
Outside the bar: clear, wind W 2

q: What is cutting the visibility, and when will it improve?
a: Frontal fog in the rain — once the front passes
o: Radiation fog — once the sun is up
Sea fog — when the wind drops to calm
Haze from a high — not for several days
why: Rain falling into cold air ahead of a warm front saturates it: frontal fog, which lifts once the front has gone through.

fig.title: Approaching the coast at night
lines: Visibility now under 1000 m in rain

q: What is the worst visibility you plan for on the leg?
a: Between 1000 m and 2 M
o: Between 2 and 5 M
Less than 1000 m
More than 5 M
why: Forecast terms: good is over 5 M, moderate 2–5 M, poor 1000 m to 2 M, fog under 1000 m.

q: How long have you got, and what do you do?
a: About 15 min — reef down and secure now
o: About 24 min — finish the leg first
About 40 min — reef once it is close
About 4 min — too late to reef now
why: 6 M at 25 kn is 0.24 h = 14.4 min, about 15 min. A squall line hits hard: reef and secure before it arrives.

fig.title: Radar, 1510
lines: Squall line on radar 6 M to the W
Your sail: full main and genoa

q: What reaches you first, and how do you prepare?
a: A cold gust from the W, ahead of the rain — reef
o: The rain, then the wind dies — keep full sail
A fresher SE breeze into the cell — ease sheets
Lightning only — the wind stays a light SE
why: Downdraughts spread out ahead of a cumulonimbus as a gust front: a sudden cold squall from the storm's side before the rain.

fig.title: Afternoon, Ionian
lines: Cumulonimbus 5 M to the W, moving E
Dark curtain of rain under the base

q: What do you check first?
a: The through-hulls and the hull for leaks
o: The VHF aerial lead at the masthead
The fridge and the cabin lights
The engine oil and coolant levels
why: A strike can blow out a through-hull or crack the hull as it leaves: look for water first, then check compass and electronics.

fig.title: Lightning strike, 1530
lines: Strike at the masthead, crew all well

q: You plan to sail along the coast under the mountains. What do these clouds warn you of?
a: Strong wind aloft — hard gusts off the high land
o: Fair weather — light winds all day
Fog forming over the sea by evening
A warm front with rain within the hour
why: Lenticular clouds form in a strong airflow over mountains: expect violent gusts down the lee slopes, even with light wind at sea.

fig.title: Corsica, morning
lines: Smooth lens-shaped clouds over the peaks
They stay put while others drift by

q: You are setting up the NAVTEX receiver before a coastal passage. Which message types can you never switch off?
a: A, B and D — nav and met warnings, SAR
o: E only — the weather forecasts
A and E — nav warnings and forecasts
B and L — met warnings and extra nav
why: NAVTEX on 518 kHz: types A (navigational warnings), B (met warnings) and D (search and rescue) cannot be rejected.

q: You are the skipper, on watch at the chart table. What do you do?
a: Switch to Ch 23, write it down, then replan
o: Note the time and wait for the 0700 forecast
Reply on Ch 16 to say you have received it
Stay on Ch 16 — the text is repeated there
why: A SÉCURITÉ on 16 announces safety information on a working channel: go there, copy it word for word, then act on it.

q: Until when, local time, could the gale arrive?
a: Any time up to 2300 local
o: Any time up to 2100 local
Any time up to 2330 local
Not before 2300 local
why: Imminent means within 6 h of issue: 1500 + 6 = 2100 UTC = 2300 local, and it can come at any time before that.

fig.title: Galicia, local time UTC+2
lines: You read it at 1730 local, at sea

q: What mean wind does the warning give?
a: 41 to 47 kn
o: 34 to 40 kn
48 to 55 kn
28 to 33 kn
why: Severe gale is force 9: a mean of 41–47 kn. Gale 8 is 34–40 kn, storm 10 is 48–55 kn.

q: How do you set the boat up for the leg?
a: Reef for gusts of about 25 kn
o: Full sail — 18 kn is only force 5
Full sail, and reef if the GRIB tops 22
One reef at 1500, when the GRIB says 18
why: A GRIB gives a model's mean wind, without gusts or local effects: 18 kn + 40 % = 25 kn in the gusts — reef for that.

fig.title: GRIB, 0.25°, 3-hourly
lines: Crew: 4, two on their first passage

q: What do you expect inside the strait?
a: More wind, along the strait — the grid misses it
o: NW 12 kn — the model covers the strait
Less wind — the islands shelter the strait
NW 12 kn, but backing W by evening
why: A 15-mile grid cannot see a 1-mile strait: funnelling between high islands is smoothed out of the GRIB.

fig.title: GRIB for the afternoon
lines: Your route: a strait 1 M wide

q: When does the front reach you, and what changes then?
a: About 1800 — a veer to NW, squalls
o: About 1800 — a back to SE and fog
About 1600 — a veer to NW, squalls
About 2400 — a veer to NW, squalls
why: 120 M at 20 kn = 6 h: about 1800 UTC. A cold front brings squalls and a sharp veer from SW to NW.

fig.title: Synoptic chart, 1200 UTC
lines: Cold front 120 M W of you
You: SW 6 in the warm sector

q: You can leave at 0600. Do you go?
a: Go — in by about 1420, the refuge as plan B
o: Stay — “later” means within 6 hours
Go at 1000 — in before the wind rises
Go — “later” means not until tomorrow
why: 50 M at 6 kn = 8 h 20 min: in by 1420. “Later” is over 12 h after issue — after 1700 — and force 6 is within this crew.

fig.title: Forecast issued 0500
lines: Your leg: 50 M at about 6 kn

q: What do you do?
a: Bear away for the refuge and reef now
o: Press on — the forecast gave 6 only later
Heave to and wait for the 0600 forecast
Press on, logging the barometer hourly
why: 5 hPa in 3 hours is ahead of the forecast: the wind is coming sooner and harder. Take the short, lit refuge off the wind.

fig.title: Night passage, 0300
lines: Refuge: 9 M on a reach, lit entrance

q: You are in the Cyclades in late July and must make a 30-mile leg due north tomorrow. When do you leave?
a: At 0500 — in by about 1100, ahead of the worst
o: At 1100 — once it has settled in for the day
At 1500 — after the midday peak has passed
At 1900 — in by 0100, as it eases off
why: The Meltemi builds from late morning to an afternoon peak: 30 M at 5 kn = 6 h, so leave at 0500 and be in by 1100.

fig.title: Cyclades, late July
lines: Builds to N 7 from about noon
Your leg: 30 M due N, 5 kn into it

q: You are in Senj in February, planning to cross 15 miles south-west to Rab today, and your crew points out that a NE wind is fair. What do you decide?
a: Stay — the Bora can hit within the hour
o: Go now — get across before it sets in
Go — NE 3 is light and fair for Rab
Go, close under the mainland for shelter
why: A cap on the Velebit, a rising glass and cold air herald the Bora: its gusts come suddenly and are worst under the mountains.

fig.title: Senj, February, 0700
lines: Cloud cap sitting on the Velebit ridge
Plan: 15 M SW across to Rab

q: You are in Kvarner, and the coastal forecast gives the Bora gusts in km/h. What do they mean in knots and on the Beaufort scale?
a: About 54 kn — storm force 10
o: About 62 kn — violent storm 11
About 28 kn — near gale 7
About 45 kn — severe gale 9
why: 100 km/h ÷ 1.852 = 54 kn: force 10 in the gusts. 62 is the figure in mph (÷ 1.609), 28 in m/s (÷ 3.6).

fig.title: Coastal forecast, Kvarner
lines: Gusts up to 100 km/h under Velebit
Your leg: 12 M along the channel

q: You plan a 30-mile leg outside the outer Croatian islands, and either of two forecasts of the same force is possible for the day. Which raises the bigger sea out there?
a: The Jugo — its fetch runs the length of the sea
o: The Bora — its gusts are far stronger
Neither — the same force gives the same sea
The Bora — cold air raises a steeper sea
why: Sea grows with fetch and duration: the Jugo blows over hundreds of miles of open Adriatic, the Bora over a few miles off the coast.
ref: Local winds — the sea they raise

fig.title: Two forecasts, same force
lines: Bora NE 7: blows off the mainland
Your leg: outside the outer islands

q: You are weatherbound in a northern Adriatic harbour after two days of Jugo. What do you prepare for next?
a: A sudden NE Bora on top of the old SE sea
o: The Jugo building again as the low deepens
A slow fall to calm and a flat sea
A SW wind veering steadily into the NW
why: When the low moves off SE, cold air pours over the mountains: a Jugo often ends in a sudden Bora, with the SE sea still running.

fig.title: Northern Adriatic, November
lines: Jugo SE 6 for two days, big SE sea
Low over Italy now moving away SE
Cloud cap forming on the mountains

q: You are bound east along this coast in a Mistral, and there are no dangers off it. Where do you meet the easiest sea?
a: A — close inshore, where the fetch is short
o: B — halfway out, clear of the gusts off the land
C — well offshore, where the wind is steady
The same everywhere — the wind is the same
why: An offshore wind has little fetch near the coast: the sea is slight close in and grows the further out you go.

q: A Mistral has kept you in Marseille since dawn, and your crew is sure it will be gone by tonight. How long do you plan to stay?
a: Days, not hours — until the Genoa low fills
o: Until tonight — a Mistral dies at sunset
Until tomorrow's sea breeze takes over
A few hours — it is only a passing squall
why: A Mistral lasts as long as the Genoa low and the high behind it hold the gradient — often several days.

fig.title: Marseille, March, 1000
lines: Low deepening over the Gulf of Genoa

q: You are coasting south on the Costa Blanca after two days of Levante and must choose a harbour for tonight. Which do you enter?
a: B — its entrance is sheltered from the swell
o: A — it is closer, and 2.5 m is only moderate
A — run in fast on the back of a wave
Anchor off A and wait for the swell to drop
why: A long Levante swell breaks on a shallow, exposed entrance: go on to the harbour whose entrance is shielded from the E.

fig.title: Costa Blanca, November
lines: Levante E 6 for two days, still blowing
Long E swell, 2.5 m and building
A: 5 M on, entrance faces E over a bar
B: 13 M on, S-facing entrance behind mole

q: You are at Bozcaada in August, planning to motor 30 miles north-east up the Dardanelles this morning. Do you set off?
a: No — a head wind on top of a foul current
o: Yes — the current sets you up the strait
Yes — the strait is sheltered from the NE
Yes, keeping to mid-channel in the lane
why: The Dardanelles current runs out to the SW; a NE Poyraz adds to it and raises a steep sea. You would make little over the ground.

fig.title: Bozcaada, August, 0700
lines: Forecast: Poyraz NE 6–7 for two days
Plan: 30 M NE up the Dardanelles
Boat: 6 kn under engine in flat water

q: Your route tomorrow runs through the strait between two Cycladic islands. Where do you expect the “locally 8” of this forecast?
a: In the straits and off the capes
o: In the lee of the high islands
In the open sea, far from land
Only in the hours before dawn
why: The Meltemi accelerates where the land squeezes it: “locally 8” falls in the straits between islands and round the capes.

fig.title: Greek forecast, Cyclades
lines: Sea 2.5 to 4 m in the open
Your route: the strait between two islands

q: You anchor at A for the night, in the lee of this high island, with a Meltemi blowing outside. What do you prepare for?
a: Hard gusts down the slopes — dig in, ample scope
o: A calm night — the island blocks the wind
A swell wrapping round from the south side
The wind backing to S as the land cools
why: In a strong Meltemi the wind spills over a high island and falls down its lee slopes in violent gusts, often worst at night.
ref: Local effects — lee of a high island

fig.note: Meltemi N 7; anchored at A from dusk

q: You are in a river marina in October and plan to leave down the river at 0700 tomorrow. What do you expect at dawn?
a: Radiation fog lying in the river valley
o: Sea fog rolling in from the coast
Frontal fog in steady rain
Clear air, as a high brings fine weather
why: A clear, calm autumn night cools the land and the air over it to the dew point: radiation fog fills the valleys by dawn.

q: On this spring evening you are heading towards colder water, with warm moist air blowing along your route. Where do you first expect fog?
a: At C — the sea there is below the dew point
o: At A — the sea is already cooler than the air
At B — within a degree of the dew point
At D — the sea must be 2°C below the dew point
why: Air over the sea cools to the sea temperature: fog forms where the sea is at or below the 12°C dew point — first at C, 11.5°C.

q: You plan to sail out of a Galician ría at 1400 for a short coastal hop. What happens to the visibility at the mouth by then?
a: The sea breeze carries the fog bank in
o: The sun burns the bank off by noon
The air off the land holds it out
It clears as the sea breeze freshens
why: The fog lies over the cold sea; the afternoon sea breeze blows it in towards the hot land and fills the mouth of the ría.
ref: Fog — sea fog and the sea breeze

fig.title: Galician ría, August, 1000
lines: Ría clear and hot, light air off the land
Fog bank lying 3 M off the mouth

q: On a night passage across the western Channel in May you log the air temperature and the dew point each hour. What do you prepare for?
a: Fog soon — radar on, fix the position, horn ready
o: Rain soon — a front is close behind
A calm soon — the breeze dies at dawn
Clearer air — the spread shows it drying
why: The air temperature has closed to within 1°C of the dew point: the air is near saturation and fog is close. Fix and prepare now.

q: You are on passage in the Channel, and a low will pass north of you tonight, fronts and all. In which order do you expect your log entries?
a: Rain, veer SW; drizzle; veer NW, showers
o: Rain, back SE; back E; back NE, showers
Showers, veer NW; drizzle; back SW, rain
Fog, back SE; rain; veer SW, drizzle
why: North of you, the warm front veers the wind S to SW with rain, the warm sector brings drizzle, the cold front a veer to NW and showers.

fig.title: Forecast for your area, 1800
lines: Low 988 moving E, centre 150 M N of you
Warm front, then cold front tonight

q: You and a friend sailed through the same night, 60 miles apart on a north–south line. Comparing logs in the morning, where did the low centre pass?
a: Between the two boats, moving E
o: North of both boats, moving E
South of both boats, moving E
Over your boat, then turning N
why: A veering wind puts the centre to your north, a backing one to your south: you veered, your friend backed — it passed between you.
ref: Depressions — the track of the centre

fig.title: Same night, two boats
lines: Friend, 60 M N: SE 6 → E 6 → NE 7

q: You are where the boat is drawn, and this low tracks east over the next 12 hours. How does your wind change?
a: It veers from about SSW through W to WNW
o: It backs from about SSW through SE to E
It stays about SSW and eases as it passes
It veers to N, then backs through W to S
why: South of a low moving E the centre goes by to your north: the wind veers, from about SSW now to W and WNW behind it.

fig.note: Low moving E, north of you

q: Your position on this morning's chart is west of the low centre. From which direction do you expect the wind?
a: From about NNW
o: From about SSE
From about ENE
From about WSW
why: Air turns anticlockwise round a northern low, angled in: on its west side it flows south, so the wind is about NNW.
ref: Pressure systems — wind round a low

q: You are planning the next two days from this chart. Which way do you expect the low centre to move?
a: ENE — along the warm-sector isobars
o: WSW — into the warm-sector wind
N — towards the cold air
SSE — across the warm-sector isobars
why: A frontal low tends to move along the isobars of its warm sector, the way the warm-sector wind blows: here to the ENE.
ref: Reading a synoptic chart — movement of a low

q: You are on an overnight coastal passage, and an occluded front will cross you around midnight. What do you expect as it passes?
a: Rain for some hours, then a veer to W and showers
o: A sudden calm and fog for the rest of the night
Steady rain, with the wind backing all night
Clear skies at once, and no rain at all
why: An occlusion acts like a warm front and a cold front together: a band of rain, then a veer and brighter, showery air.

fig.title: Forecast, 1800
lines: Ahead of it: SE 5, barometer falling

q: You are on a night passage, and the log shows this since midnight. What weather do you plan for the rest of the night?
a: Gusty NW with showers and good visibility
o: Steady rain, with the SW wind returning
Fog, as the clear air cools over the sea
A calm, then a slow back to the SE
why: A squall, a sharp veer and a jump in pressure: the cold front has passed. Behind it comes cold, gusty NW air with showers.

fig.title: Night log
lines: 0400 rain stopped, stars to the W

q: You must make a 45-mile leg to the south-east some time in the next three days. Which day do you sail?
a: Day 2 — a fair NW 4–5 and good visibility
o: Day 1 — sail before the front arrives
Night 1 — ride the front through fast
Day 3 — once the next low has settled
why: Behind the cold front a NW wind is on your quarter for a SE leg, in clear air; day 1 runs into the front, day 3 into the next low.
ref: Reading a synoptic chart — a 48 h plan

fig.title: Forecast for the next 3 days
lines: Day 1: warm sector, SW 6, poor vis
Night 1: cold front, squalls, veer NW

q: You are anchored off the coast and read this at midnight. Between which times could the low centre reach you?
a: From about 1130 to 1600 UTC
o: From about 0900 to 1130 UTC
From about 1600 to 0240 UTC
Not before about 0300 UTC tomorrow
why: “Rather quickly” is 25–35 kn: 400 M takes 11.4 to 16 h, so about 1130 to 1600 UTC. 15–25 kn would be “steadily”.

fig.title: Synoptic chart, 0000 UTC
lines: Low 980 hPa, 400 M to the W of you
You: anchored, open to the S and W

q: You are reading the forecast for your area before a coastal passage. What does the word “cyclonic” warn you of?
a: Big, quick shifts of wind near a passing centre
o: A steady wind from one direction all day
Light winds circling a high over you
A tropical storm on its way to you
why: “Cyclonic” means the centre of a low passes over or close to the area: the wind changes direction a lot, and quickly.

q: You hear this gale warning just before leaving on a 7-hour coastal leg. Could the gale catch you at sea?
a: Yes — it could arrive from about 1200 UTC
o: No — not before 1800 UTC at the earliest
No — “soon” means 12 to 24 hours ahead
Yes — at any moment in the next hour
why: “Soon” is 6 to 12 hours from issue: from 1200 to 1800 UTC — well inside your time at sea.

q: You measure the isobar spacing over your area on the synoptic chart. What surface wind do you plan for at sea?
a: About 32 kn — F7
o: About 48 kn — F10
About 16 kn — F4
About 8 kn — F3
why: Half the spacing doubles the wind: 24 × 100/50 = 48 kn geostrophic; × ⅔ at the surface = 32 kn, force 7.

fig.title: Synoptic chart, isobars every 4 hPa
lines: Surface wind at sea: about ⅔ of that
Over your area: isobars 50 M apart

q: Your chart's geostrophic scale is drawn for 50°N, but you are sailing at 40°N in the Mediterranean. What does the same isobar spacing give you?
a: More — about 24 kn
o: Less — about 17 kn
The same — 20 kn
Less — about 13 kn
why: The same gradient blows harder nearer the equator: 20 × 0.77 / 0.64 = 24 kn at 40°N.

q: You are writing up the log at midnight and must describe the barometer in forecast terms. Which word fits the tendency?
a: Falling quickly
o: Falling slowly
Falling
Falling very rapidly
why: 4.5 hPa in 3 h: “slowly” is under 1.6, “falling” 1.6–3.5, “quickly” 3.6–6.0, “very rapidly” over 6.0.

q: Your crew says the boat's barometer reads wrong, so its fall tonight means nothing. What do you tell them?
a: The 5 hPa fall in 3 h is real — prepare now
o: It reads 3 high, so the fall is only 2 hPa
An aneroid that reads high is no use at all
Wait for the coastguard's next report
why: A constant error does not change the tendency: 1011 to 1006 is 5 hPa in 3 h, well past 3 — strong wind is on its way.

q: You are on a night passage with 20 miles to go at about 5 knots, and you read back the barometer log at 0500. What does it tell you?
a: A slow fall — carry on, in by 0900, keep logging
o: A fast fall — run for shelter now
A rise — the low has already passed
No change — stop logging it until dawn
why: 1.5 hPa every 3 h is “falling slowly”: the change is many hours off. 20 M at 5 kn = 4 h, in by 0900 — but keep watching.

q: You are anchored at A at dusk, lying to a light breeze off the beach, as a thunderstorm comes in from the west over the sea. What do you do?
a: Re-anchor further out before the gust arrives
o: Stay — the anchor is well set for the E breeze
Shorten the chain so that you swing less
Take everyone ashore until it has passed
why: The gust front will swing you 180° towards the beach: 30 m of chain from 40 m off leaves no room. Move out now.

q: You are anchored for the night and time the thunder after each flash. How far off is the storm now, and is it closing?
a: About 3 km, closing at about 16 kn
o: About 9 km, closing at about 48 kn
About 3 km, and moving away from you
About 5 km, closing at about 16 kn
why: 9 s ÷ 3 = 3 km now, 15 s ÷ 3 = 5 km before: 2 km in 4 min is 30 km/h, about 16 kn towards you.

fig.title: Storm to the W, you at anchor

q: You are anchored in a bay under high mountains on a still August day. When, and from where, do you expect trouble?
a: Late afternoon — squalls off the mountains
o: At dawn — squalls from the open sea
At noon — as the sea breeze peaks
Not today — the sky clears by 1600
why: Daytime heating builds cumulonimbus over high ground; the storms break late in the day and their gusts pour down off the hills.

q: You are alone on watch at 0200 under full sail and notice these signs to windward. What is your first move?
a: Call the skipper and reef now
o: Hold on — the wind drops under the cloud
Wait until lightning shows you the cloud
Bear away to outrun the cloud
why: A black, starless sky to windward with cold air and lightning is a squall on its way: reef before it, not in it.

q: Before a 30-mile leg along a coast of headlands, the GRIB on your tablet and the official coastal forecast disagree. Which do you plan on?
a: The official forecast — reef for F6–7
o: The GRIB — its numbers are more precise
The average of the two — about F5
The GRIB — it shows the wind hour by hour
why: The official forecast is a forecaster's reading of several models and local effects; a raw GRIB is one model's mean wind.
ref: GRIB files vs the official forecast

q: You plan to leave at 0800 tomorrow on a 60-mile leg, and two weather models disagree about the cold front. How do you plan?
a: Wait — on model A the front meets your arrival
o: Go — model B gives you the whole day
Go — split them, the front comes at midnight
Go — the model with the finer grid is right
why: 60 M at 6 kn = 10 h: in at 1800, just as model A brings the front. When models disagree, plan on the earlier one.

fig.title: Two models, the same cold front
lines: Model A: front through at 1800 tomorrow
Model B: front through at 0600 next day
Squalls and a veer to NW 7 with it
Your leg: 60 M at 6 kn from 0800

q: Your crew shows you the GRIB they downloaded in port three days ago. Which forecast do you plan today's leg on?
a: The NAVTEX — it is the newest forecast
o: The GRIB — it was made for today
The GRIB — it gives one exact number
Neither — the sky and the barometer
why: A forecast loses accuracy with age: a three-day-old model run is out of date. Plan on the latest official forecast.
ref: GRIB files — age of the forecast

fig.title: Chart table, 0700
lines: GRIB from 3 days ago: NW 10 kn today

q: You zoom in on the GRIB at your next waypoint and read this wind barb. What wind does it show?
a: SW 25 kn
o: NE 25 kn
SW 30 kn
SW 15 kn
why: A barb points into the wind, here from the SW; each long feather is 10 kn and a short one 5: 10 + 10 + 5 = 25 kn.

fig.title: GRIB wind barb at the waypoint
lines: Shaft runs from the dot towards the SW
Two long feathers, one short feather
Feathers at the far end of the shaft

q: You are planning an open-water leg of six hours under this forecast. What are the biggest waves you should be ready for?
a: About 6 m, now and then
o: About 3 m, as forecast
About 4 m, now and then
About 9 m, now and then
why: The forecast height is the significant wave height; over a few hours single waves of nearly twice that will come through.

q: You are working out the sea you will meet on the leg from the two parts of this forecast. About how high is the combined sea?
a: About 2.5 m
o: About 3.5 m
About 2.0 m
About 0.5 m
why: √(2.0² + 1.5²) = √6.25 = 2.5 m. The two heights do not simply add, and the swell alone is not the whole sea.
ref: Sea state — swell and wind sea

q: You are running dead downwind in a 12 m catamaran, and the instrument shows the apparent wind. What does the reefing chart tell you to do?
a: Reef 1 now — the true wind is about 23 kn
o: No reef — 14 kn is under the first reef
Reef 2 now — the true wind is about 28 kn
No reef — the true wind is about 5 kn
why: Dead downwind the true wind is the apparent plus boat speed: 14 + 9 = 23 kn, past the 18 kn first reef but short of 24.

fig.title: Catamaran, running dead downwind
lines: Boat speed 9 kn, apparent wind 14 kn
Reef chart: 1st reef at 18 kn true
A cat does not heel to warn you

q: You are beating at night and must log the true wind force from the instruments. What do you write?
a: About 19 kn — F5
o: About 24 kn — F6
About 30 kn — F7
About 14 kn — F4
why: Take the boat's speed out of the apparent wind: along the bow 24 × 0.82 − 6 = 13.7, across 24 × 0.57 = 13.7; √ = 19 kn.
ref: Beaufort — the true wind at night

fig.title: Night, close-hauled
lines: Apparent wind 24 kn, 35° off the bow

q: Your crew thinks a rise from 16 to 24 knots adds only half as much again to the load on the rig. What do you tell them?
a: About 2¼ times — reef now
o: About 1½ times — no change yet
About 3½ times — drop all sail
About the same — the boat heels it off
why: Wind load goes with the square of the speed: (24 / 16)² = 2.25, not 1.5. Reef for it.

fig.title: Wind rising on passage
lines: Force on the sails goes as wind²

q: Your track crosses this offshore bank, and the forecast has just been upgraded. What do you do?
a: Route round the bank — the sea may break on it
o: Cross it — 6 m is plenty for a 2 m draft
Cross it near high water, for more depth
Cross it fast, to be over it sooner
why: Waves steepen and break where the depth falls to about their height: 3–4 m seas, and the bigger ones, will break on a 6 m bank.

q: You are bound west round the Point today with a westerly force 6 blowing. At which of these times off the Point would the sea be worst?
why: The W-going stream runs against a W wind, at its strongest at HW+4: 1040 + 4 h = 1440. At 0840 the stream runs with the wind.
ref: Wind against tide — timing at a headland

fig.title: Off the Point, springs
lines: W-going stream: HW+1 to HW+7, max HW+4

q: You will round this headland at A this afternoon, while the spring stream runs west. What sea do you expect there?
a: Short, steep and breaking — rough, not moderate
o: Moderate, as forecast — the stream makes no odds
Flatter than forecast — the stream smooths it
A long, low swell rolling in from the W
why: A W wind over a W-going stream is wind against tide: the waves shorten and steepen, and off a headland they break.

q: You plan to sail 8 miles out from this south-facing coast and back this afternoon. What wind do you expect out there?
a: A calm belt offshore, where the two winds meet
o: A strong S breeze — the N wind adds to it
The N 3 all day — it stops the sea breeze
A sea breeze from the N, off the land
why: A light offshore gradient holds the sea breeze back; where the two meet, a few miles out, lies a belt of calm, fickle air.
ref: Sea breeze — against an offshore wind

fig.title: South-facing coast, July
lines: Gradient wind: N 3, off the land
Sea breeze expected from the S by 1300

q: You are coasting towards a harbour whose entrance faces south over a shallow bar. When do you plan to arrive?
a: In the morning, before the sea breeze sets in
o: Mid-afternoon, with the breeze behind you
At 1300, while the breeze is still young
At dusk, while the sea is still running
why: The sea breeze blows onshore through the afternoon and builds a short sea on the bar: arrive in the calm of the morning.

fig.title: Approach, Turkish coast, August
lines: Entrance faces S, over a shallow bar
Mornings: calm or light N off the land
Sea breeze S 5 from about 1200 to 1800
Short steep sea builds on the bar

q: You are cruising in Greek waters and want the NAVTEX weather in English. Which frequency do you select on the receiver?
a: 518 kHz
o: 490 kHz
why: 518 kHz is the international NAVTEX service, in English; 490 kHz carries the national-language broadcasts.
